claim: TANGO1 organises membranes at the interface of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and ERGIC/Golgi.
source: We have previously shown TANGO1 organises membranes at the interface of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and ERGIC/Golgi (Raote et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Raote et al., 2018

claim: TANGO1 corrals retrograde membranes at ER exit sites to create an export conduit.
source: TANGO1 corrals retrograde membranes at ER exit sites to create an export conduit.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Raote et al., 2018) mentioned in the abstract

claim: The retrograde membrane is, in itself, an anterograde carrier.
source: Here the retrograde membrane is, in itself, an anterograde carrier.
evidence: Based on the authors' interpretation of their previous findings

claim: TANGO1 has one membrane-spanning helix (TM) and another helix that penetrates the inner leaflet (IM).
source: TANGO1 has an unusual membrane helix organisation, composed of one membrane-spanning helix (TM) and another that penetrates the inner leaflet (IM).
evidence: Structural characterization of TANGO1 membrane helices

claim: TM and IM together reduce the flow of lipids at a region of defined shape in model membranes.
source: We have reconstituted these membrane helices in model membranes and shown that TM and IM together reduce the flow of lipids at a region of defined shape.
evidence: Experimental data from reconstitution experiments shown in Figure 2

claim: The helices align TANGO1 around an ER exit site.
source: We have also shown that the helices align TANGO1 around an ER exit site.
evidence: Experimental data from STED microscopy shown in Figure 4

claim: Membrane curvature plays a major role in lipid and protein sorting during transport intermediate formation.
source: a key question is whether (and how) membrane curvature plays a major role in lipid and protein sorting (Campelo and Malhotra, 2012).
evidence: Cited as an open question in the field

claim: Curvature-mediated lipid sorting requires additional protein-lipid interactions beyond curvature alone.
source: current evidence suggests that curvature-mediated lipid sorting is not based on curvature alone, but requires additional protein-lipid interactions (Brügger et al., 2000; Callan-Jones et al., 2011; Gruenberg, 2003; Klemm et al., 2009; Roux et al., 2005; Sorre et al., 2009; Tian and Baumgart, 2009).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies

claim: COPII vesicles show enrichment in lysolipids such as lysophosphatidylinositol (LPI) and a decrease in phosphatidylserine compared to the ER.
source: In vitro preparations of COPII vesicles show a differential lipidomic profile from the ER, including an enrichment in lysolipids such as lysophosphatidylinositol (LPI) and a decrease in phosphatidylserine (Melero et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Melero et al., 2018

claim: ERES are semi-stable specialized subdomains of the ER with pleomorphic organization of diverse curvatures, including cup-like shapes and beaded tubes.
source: COPII vesicles form at ER exit sites (ERES), which are semi-stable specialized subdomains of the ER with structures of a pleomorphic organization of diverse curvatures, including cup-like shapes and beaded tubes (Bannykh et al., 1996; Hughes et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bannykh et al., 1996 and Hughes et al., 2009

claim: Procollagens fold and trimerize into rigid, rod-like elements that are considered too large for conventional COPII coated vesicle-mediated transport.
source: Procollagens in the ER fold and trimerize into rigid, rod-like elements that are considered too large for conventional COPII coated vesicle-mediated transport (Burgeson et al., 1985; Gorur et al., 2017; Kadler, 2017; Kadler et al., 2007; McCaughey and Stephens, 2019; Omari et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies

claim: Large COPII-coated carriers were reported in cells overexpressing KLHL12.
source: Outsize COPII carriers were reported in cells overexpressing KLHL12, which generates large procollagen-containing structures that co-label with Sec31A (Jin et al., 2012; Yuan et al., 2017; Yuan et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jin et al., 2012; Yuan et al., 2017; Yuan et al., 2018

claim: Large procollagen-containing structures generated by KLHL12 overexpression are destined for degradation and not bona fide transport carriers.
source: A subsequent report suggested that these structures are destined for degradation and not bona fide transport carriers (Omari et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Omari et al., 2018

claim: ER-to-Golgi procollagen carriers appear pleomorphic and do not seem to contain any detectable COPII.
source: However, ER-to-Golgi procollagen carriers appear pleomorphic and do not seem to contain any detectable COPII (Mironov et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mironov et al., 2003

claim: Procollagen export from the ER requires the assembly of a functional machine centred on the transmembrane ERES-resident protein TANGO1.
source: Procollagen export from the ER requires the assembly of a functional machine centred on the transmembrane ERES-resident protein TANGO1 (Ishikawa et al., 2016; Lekszas et al., 2020; Saito et al., 2009; Wilson et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies

claim: TANGO1 acts as a filamentous linactant to recruit, constrain, and scaffold ERES machinery and post-ER (ERGIC) membranes for procollagen export.
source: As a master regulator of ERES assembly, TANGO1 acts as a filamentous linactant to recruit, constrain, and scaffold ERES machinery and post-ER (ERGIC) membranes for procollagen export (Ma and Goldberg, 2016; Maeda et al., 2017; Nogueira et al., 2014; Raote et al., 2017; Raote et al., 2018; Raote et al., 2019; Saito and Maeda, 2019; Saito et al., 2009; Santos et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies

claim: TANGO1 utilises a retrograde membrane tether complex (NRZ complex) to tether post-ER membranes (ERGIC/Golgi), which fuse at the ERES to create an export route for procollagens.
source: Instead, TANGO1 utilises a retrograde membrane tether complex (NRZ complex) to tether post-ER membranes (ERGIC/Golgi), which fuse at the ERES to create an export route for procollagens.
evidence: Based on the authors' previous work and model

claim: TANGO1 assembles into a filament-like ring to organise the early secretory pathway.
source: Using super-resolution (STED) microscopy to visualise TANGO1, its interactors, and associated machinery we have described its assembly into a filament-like ring to organise the early secretory pathway (Liu et al., 2017; Raote and Malhotra, 2019; Raote et al., 2017; Raote et al., 2018; Raote et al., 2019; Reynolds et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies by the authors

claim: Amino acid residues 1177–1197 of human TANGO1 are predicted to form a transmembrane helix.
source: amino acid residues 1177–1197 of human TANGO1 are predicted to form a transmembrane helix, while residues 1145–1165 form a helix that penetrates the lumenal leaflet of the ER membrane (Saito et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Saito et al., 2009

claim: Amino acid residues 1145–1165 of human TANGO1 form a helix that penetrates the lumenal leaflet of the ER membrane.
source: amino acid residues 1177–1197 of human TANGO1 are predicted to form a transmembrane helix, while residues 1145–1165 form a helix that penetrates the lumenal leaflet of the ER membrane (Saito et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Saito et al., 2009

claim: Similar levels of protein were incorporated into GUVs in the IM-TM and TM conditions.
source: To confirm that similar levels of protein were incorporated into GUVs in the two conditions tested, we compared the intensities of IM-TM and TM in the GUVs and found that they are similar under the same conditions of microscope objective, laser power and gain: 92 ± 23 a.u. for IM-TM and 106 ± 38 a.u. for TM respectively.
evidence: Quantitative fluorescence intensity measurements from GUV experiments

claim: The protein to lipid ratio in the GUVs is approximately 1 IM-TM protein per 18,000 lipids.
source: Under our conditions, we estimate 1 IM-TM protein per 18,000 lipids, that is a typical inter-protein distance of 80 nm (see Materials and methods section for a more detailed description of this quantification).
evidence: Calculated from fluorescence intensity measurements

claim: Fluorescence recovered to 60 ± 6% of the prebleach intensity in tubes from GUVs with no protein.
source: Fluorescence recovered to 60 ± 6% (mean ±s.d.) of the prebleach intensity in tubes from GUVs with no protein.
evidence: Experimental data from photobleaching recovery experiments shown in Figure 2

claim: In tubes pulled from GUVs with the transmembrane helix alone (TM), fluorescence recovered to 56 ± 12%.
source: Similarly, in tubes pulled from GUVs with the transmembrane helix alone (TM), fluorescence recovered to 56 ± 12%.
evidence: Experimental data from photobleaching recovery experiments shown in Figure 2

claim: The two helices together (IM-TM) reduced fluorescence recovery to only 35 ± 5%.
source: However, the two helices together (IM-TM), considerably inhibited fluorescence recovery. Now, the recovery was only 35 ± 5% (Figure 2C), showing that TANGO1 membrane helices together inhibited the exchange of lipids between the tube and the rest of the GUV.
evidence: Experimental data from photobleaching recovery experiments shown in Figure 2

claim: TANGO1 membrane helices together inhibited the exchange of lipids between the tube and the rest of the GUV.
source: showing that TANGO1 membrane helices together inhibited the exchange of lipids between the tube and the rest of the GUV.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental data from photobleaching recovery experiments

claim: The diffusion coefficient of EGFP-labeled protein in the GUV is 0.7 ± 0.3 µm²/s.
source: We found a diffusion coefficient (0.7 ± 0.3 µm²/s), consistent with a protein that is monomeric or in the form of small oligomers (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Experimental data from FRAP experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: The measured diffusion coefficient is consistent with a protein that is monomeric or in the form of small oligomers.
source: We found a diffusion coefficient (0.7 ± 0.3 µm²/s), consistent with a protein that is monomeric or in the form of small oligomers (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Interpretation of diffusion coefficient measurement based on established knowledge

claim: The membrane (protein and lipid) is fully fluid without hindered diffusion.
source: These data show that the membrane (protein and lipid) is fully fluid without hindered diffusion, confirming that the low recovery in the tube is due to reduced crossing at the junction between the GUV and the tube.
evidence: Interpretation of FRAP data

claim: The low recovery in the tube is due to reduced crossing at the junction between the GUV and the tube.
source: confirming that the low recovery in the tube is due to reduced crossing at the junction between the GUV and the tube.
evidence: Inference from FRAP and photobleaching recovery data

claim: Deletion of the IM helix had no discernible effect on the ability of TANGO1 to localise to ERES.
source: Deletion of the IM helix had no discernible effect on the ability of TANGO1 (Figure 3B, green) to localise to ERES as visualised by its localisation to puncta of the ERES marker Sec16A (Figure 3B, red).
evidence: Experimental data from immunofluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 3B

claim: Deletion of the TM helix resulted in a loss of TANGO1 localisation to ERES.
source: Deletion of the TM helix had a more substantive effect and resulted in a loss of TANGO1 localisation to ERES (Figure 3A,B, quantified in 3C).
evidence: Experimental data from immunofluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 3

claim: When the TM in TANGO1 is deleted, the IM changes its topology and becomes a transmembrane helix.
source: We have previously shown that when the TM in TANGO1 is deleted, the IM changes its topology and becomes a transmembrane.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: Deleting both hydrophobic helices leads to a soluble protein in the ER lumen.
source: Deleting both hydrophobic helices leads to a soluble protein in the ER lumen (Saito et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Saito et al., 2009

claim: Deleting either helix had no effect on targeting TANGO1 to accumulations of procollagen VII in the ER.
source: As a control, we confirmed that deleting either helix had no effect on targeting TANGO1 to accumulations of procollagen VII in the ER (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Experimental data from immunofluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Both TANGO1 and TANGO1ΔIM were recruited as small, discrete puncta, which were apposed to collagen accumulations in the ER.
source: Both TANGO1 and TANGO1ΔIM were recruited as small, discrete puncta, which were apposed to collagen accumulations in the ER.
evidence: Experimental observation from immunofluorescence microscopy

claim: TANGO1ΔTM entirely overlapped with procollagen VII accumulations.
source: The TANGO1ΔTM entirely overlapped with procollagen VII accumulations.
evidence: Experimental observation from immunofluorescence microscopy

claim: Membrane curvature/shape sensitivity in TANGO1 membrane helices is not the dominant ERES-targeting device.
source: Together, these data reveal that membrane curvature/shape sensitivity in TANGO1 membrane helices is not the dominant ERES-targeting device, instead the PRD is more important to target TANGO1 to its cellular location at an ERES.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental data from Figure 3

claim: The PRD is more important to target TANGO1 to its cellular location at an ERES.
source: instead the PRD is more important to target TANGO1 to its cellular location at an ERES.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental data and previous knowledge

claim: TANGO1 can be visualised assembled into rings at ERES.
source: TANGO1 can be visualised assembled into rings at ERES (Raote et al., 2017; Raote et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies by the authors

claim: There was a clear separation of the signal from antibodies directed against the lumenal and cytoplasmic epitopes of TANGO1.
source: Under these conditions there was a clear separation of the signal from antibodies directed against the two different epitopes and we could identify two distinct configurations of the ring of TANGO1.
evidence: Experimental observation from STED microscopy shown in Figure 4

claim: Two distinct configurations of the TANGO1 ring were identified: either the C terminus coalesced into a single spot within a ring formed by the lumenal antibody, or both could be visualised as concentric/colocalized rings.
source: Either the C terminus coalesced into a single spot within a ring formed by the lumenal antibody, or both could be visualised as concentric/colocalized rings (Figure 4A red vs. green respectively).
evidence: Experimental observation from STED microscopy shown in Figure 4A

claim: The distinct sets of images represented discrete configurations of TANGO1 during the formation of a carrier at an ERES.
source: We propose that these distinct sets of images represented discrete configurations of TANGO1 during the formation of a carrier at an ERES.
evidence: Authors' interpretation of STED microscopy data

claim: Initially, the C termini of TANGO1 lie within the ring, overlying the site of the formation of a carrier.
source: Initially, the C termini of TANGO1 lie within the ring, overlying the site of the formation of a carrier. As the carrier grows, the C termini are gradually pushed apart (for a schematic, Figure 4D).
evidence: Authors' model based on STED microscopy observations

claim: As the carrier grows, the C termini are gradually pushed apart.
source: As the carrier grows, the C termini are gradually pushed apart (for a schematic, Figure 4D).
evidence: Authors' model based on STED microscopy observations

claim: Abrogating the intramembrane helix reduced the frequency with which rings were observed.
source: Qualitatively, we observed that abrogating the intramembrane helix reduced the frequency with which we observed rings, but this observation could not be quantified given the subjective nature of the selection of fields to image.
evidence: Qualitative observation from STED microscopy

claim: In several of the rings that did form with TANGO1ΔIM, the C termini (HA epitope) and lumenal portions of TANGO1 were misaligned.
source: Interestingly, in several of the rings that did form, the C termini (HA epitope) and lumenal portions of TANGO1 were now misaligned (Figure 4B).
evidence: Experimental observation from STED microscopy shown in Figure 4B

claim: With TANGO1ΔIM, the C termini were often randomly oriented with respect to the ring formed by the lumenal epitope.
source: Now, the C termini were often randomly oriented with respect to the ring formed by the lumenal epitope.
evidence: Experimental observation from STED microscopy

claim: Mutating two hydrophobic residues in the IM helix to charged residues (phenylalanine 1152 and 1154 to arginine – TANGO1-FMF-RMR) resulted in many rings of TANGO1 showing altered alignment of the two epitopes.
source: Alternatively, we mutated two hydrophobic residues in the IM helix to charged residues (phenylalanine 1152 and 1154 to arginine – TANGO1-FMF-RMR), such that it would no longer form a hydrophobic helix (Figure 4—figure supplement 1). Here too, many rings of TANGO1 showed altered alignment of the two epitopes.
evidence: Experimental observation from STED microscopy shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Ring formation could create a feedback loop through orientation/shape sensing to further reinforce rings.
source: In other words, ring formation could create a feedback loop through orientation/shape sensing to further reinforce rings.
evidence: Authors' speculation based on their model

claim: The transmembrane organisation of TANGO1 is sufficient to act as a diffusion barrier for membrane lipids.
source: We showed that the transmembrane organisation of TANGO1 is sufficient to act as a diffusion barrier for membrane lipids.
evidence: Conclusion from experimental data in Figure 2

claim: TANGO1 is concentrated at the neck of a budding membrane and can act as a fence, constraining the flow of lipids.
source: In doing so, our data suggest that TANGO1 is concentrated at the neck of a budding membrane and can act as a fence, constraining the flow of lipids.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental data

claim: Cargo transport through the secretory pathway can be mediated by transient tunnels or pores between successive compartments.
source: We have proposed that cargo transport through the secretory pathway can be mediated by transient tunnels or pores between successive compartments (Raote and Malhotra, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by the authors

claim: Retrograde fusion of ERGIC membrane to the ER could create a tunnel between the two compartments for procollagen export.
source: We have shown that retrograde fusion of ERGIC membrane to the ER could create a tunnel between the two compartments for procollagen export (Nogueira et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nogueira et al., 2014

claim: PI4P is required at the ERGIC-ERES interface to assist in the assembly of COPII‐coated vesicles at ERES.
source: Lipids such as PI4P are required at the ERGIC-ERES interface to assist in the assembly of COPII‐coated vesicles at ERES and hence traffic from the ER (Blumental-Perry et al., 2006; Farhan et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Blumental-Perry et al., 2006 and Farhan et al., 2008

claim: 50–75% of the saddle is blocked by the membrane helices based on recovery rates observed.
source: The lipid flux through the partial barrier between the GUV and the tube is proportional to the effective perimeter of the saddle. From the recovery rates observed in Figure 2, then 50–75% of the saddle is blocked by the membrane helices.
evidence: Calculation based on experimental data from Figure 2

claim: There are approximately 172,000 molecules of TANGO1 per cell.
source: There are ~172,000 molecules of TANGO1 and 250–500 exit sites per cell or 350–700 TANGO1 molecules per exit site, surrounding transport intermediates (Hammond and Glick, 2000; Itzhak et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hammond and Glick, 2000 and Itzhak et al., 2016

claim: There are 250–500 exit sites per cell.
source: There are ~172,000 molecules of TANGO1 and 250–500 exit sites per cell or 350–700 TANGO1 molecules per exit site, surrounding transport intermediates (Hammond and Glick, 2000; Itzhak et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hammond and Glick, 2000 and Itzhak et al., 2016

claim: There are 350–700 TANGO1 molecules per exit site.
source: There are ~172,000 molecules of TANGO1 and 250–500 exit sites per cell or 350–700 TANGO1 molecules per exit site, surrounding transport intermediates (Hammond and Glick, 2000; Itzhak et al., 2016).
evidence: Calculation based on cited data

claim: By assembling into a ring at an ERES, TANGO1 can act to reduce lipid flow at the boundary between the ER and ERGIC compartments.
source: Our data presented here suggest that by assembling into a ring at an ERES, TANGO1 can act to reduce lipid flow at the boundary between the two compartments, delaying lipid and most likely transmembrane protein mixing between them.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental data

claim: TANGO1 assembly into a ring delays lipid and most likely transmembrane protein mixing between the ER and ERGIC.
source: Our data presented here suggest that by assembling into a ring at an ERES, TANGO1 can act to reduce lipid flow at the boundary between the two compartments, delaying lipid and most likely transmembrane protein mixing between them.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental data with speculation about transmembrane proteins

claim: The recruitment of TANGO1 to membrane regions of specific shape and curvature will make for greater efficiency in generating a bud at an ERES.
source: We envisage that the recruitment of TANGO1 to membrane regions of specific shape and curvature will make for greater efficiency in generating a bud at an ERES.
evidence: Authors' speculation based on their findings

claim: Neighbouring TANGO1 molecules in the ER membrane will align along curved membrane found at an ERES.
source: Neighbouring TANGO1 molecules in the ER membrane will align along curved membrane - found at an ERES.
evidence: Authors' model based on their findings

claim: The process whereby a TANGO1 fence limits the coat polymerisation zone could be homologous to the roles played by proteins FCHO1/2 and EPS15/EPSR in clathrin-mediated endocytosis.
source: This process, whereby a TANGO1 fence limiting the coat polymerisation zone, could be homologous to the roles played by proteins which contribute to the initiation of clathrin-mediated endocytosis FCHO1/2 and EPS15/EPSR (Avinoam et al., 2015; Ma et al., 2016).
evidence: Speculation based on analogy to other systems, supported by citations

claim: Hundreds of TANGO1 molecules at each site will have an additive or even synergistic effect in stabilising the bud.
source: Hundreds of TANGO1 molecules, at each site, will have an additive or even synergistic effect in stabilising the bud.
evidence: Authors' speculation based on their model

claim: Increased membrane curvature will promote the recruitment and localisation of curvature-sensitive components including Sar1 and COPII coat proteins.
source: As the site of budding is defined, the increased membrane curvature will promote the recruitment and localisation of curvature-sensitive components including Sar1 and COPII coat proteins.
evidence: Authors' model based on their findings and established knowledge

claim: Curvature-sensitive components will serve to reinforce the curvature stabilisation, setting up a positive feedback loop.
source: These proteins will serve to reinforce the curvature stabilisation, in effect setting up a positive feedback loop, where exit site machinery and TANGO1 mutually recruit and constrain each other through their membrane sculpting capabilities.
evidence: Authors' model based on their findings

claim: Aligned TANGO1 molecules will be constrained into a configuration in which it is more likely for them to participate in lateral interactions with each other.
source: Aligned TANGO1 molecules will be constrained into a configuration in which it is more likely for them to participate in lateral interactions with each other, promoting their assembly into a filament, further reinforcing the organisation of TANGO1 and its interactors at the site.
evidence: Authors' model based on their findings

claim: Only half of the rings of TANGO1ΔIM show detectable signal outside the ring from the C-terminal epitope.
source: These reinforcing activities are evident from our data, showing that only half of the rings of TANGO1ΔIM show detectable signal outside the ring from the C-terminal epitope (Figure 4).

claim: Each ring is likely comprised of hundreds of TANGO1ΔIM molecules.
source: Each ring is likely comprised of hundreds, of TANGO1ΔIM molecules.

claim: For signal from the two different epitopes to appear normal, most molecules must be constrained in the correct orientation, probably by the combined effects of other proteins at the site including COPII components and other TANGO1 family proteins.
source: For signal from the two different epitopes to appear normal, most molecules must be constrained in the correct orientation, probably by the combined effects of other proteins at the site including COPII components and other TANGO1 family proteins.
evidence: Authors' interpretation of STED microscopy data

claim: The recruitment/stabilisation of TANGO1 at a region of defined saddle-like shape may contribute partially to the retention of TANGO1 in the ER instead of accompanying cargo to the next secretory compartment.
source: It is possible that the recruitment/stabilisation of TANGO1 at a region of defined saddle-like shape will contribute partially to the retention of TANGO1 in the ER instead of accompanying cargo to the next secretory compartment.

source: an alternatively spliced short variant of TANGO1 (TANGO1-short) lacks lumenal domains, but still has two helices though its IM helix has a different sequence.

claim: In TMEM131, one helix must span the membrane, while the other is likely inserted into one leaflet of a compartment membrane.

claim: TANGO1 interacts with coats and other cytoplasmic components that tether and transiently fuse ERES to ERGIC or the cis-Golgi.
source: and interacts with coats and other cytoplasmic components that tether and transiently fuse ERES to ERGIC or the cis-Golgi (in cells that lack an ERGIC).

source: The transmembrane helices in TANGO1 assist in its alignment into a ring to prevent membrane protein and lipid mixing during the transient coupling of these two secretory compartments.
